# Psalm 87: Verse-by-Verse Notes

**Gaps:** I didn't find NET Bible or Bible Odyssey notes, Orthodox (OCA) material, Lutheran sources, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this psalm. Those are left out. My research ran out before I could read Spurgeon's full Psalm 87 page, so only the parts I saw are used.

---

**v. 1: "He has founded His city on the holy mountains"**

*Traditional reading*
- Guzik: God owns the whole earth and isn't a local god, but He has a special regard for Jerusalem. Quoting Kidner, he says the hills are holy because God is there, not the reverse. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-87/
- Coffman makes the same point. God is not there because the mountains are holy, but they are holy because God is there. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/87-1.html
- Clarke says the city stood mainly on two hills, Zion and Moriah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/87-1.html
- Pulpit Commentary: "holy mountains" means the hill country of Judea, holy because it surrounds the holy city. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-87.html

*Where readers differ*
- Some Jewish writers took "His foundation" as part of the title, meaning "the subject of this song." Barnes calls this a forced and unnatural interpretation and says "His" refers to God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/87-1.html
- Calvin (Reformed) also rejects the title reading. He says the plain sense is that God chose the holy mountains as the place to found His city. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/87-1.html
- Gill (Baptist) reads the verse spiritually. The mountains can stand for God's firm decrees, especially election, and the covenant of grace, but "especially" for Christ, the sure foundation laid in Zion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/87-1.htm
- Matthew Henry: Christ is the church's foundation, and holiness is what keeps the church steady. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/87-1.html
- Ellicott (Anglican) notes that because the opening has no verb, some suspect a line has dropped out. He thinks that's unnecessary if you read "gates of Zion" as the same thing as "His foundation." https://biblehub.com/psalms/87-1.htm

**v. 2: "The LORD loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob"**

- Pulpit Commentary: "the other dwellings" means places like Shiloh and Kirjath-jearim, where the ark rested before. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-87.html
- Guzik gives reasons for God's special love of Jerusalem, from Melchizedek to the cross and Pentecost. He adds that God will make it the physical centre of His future kingdom on earth. This future-literal emphasis is his own and isn't shared by the older church-focused commentators below. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-87/
- A Pulpit homily says God loved Zion more than other homes in Israel because His glory, grace and truth were most clearly shown there. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-87.html

**v. 3: "Glorious things are ascribed to you, O city of God. Selah"**

- Pulpit Commentary: the psalmist is likely thinking partly of earlier prophecies and partly of what he is about to reveal in verses 4–7. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-87.html
- Guzik mentions Boice's view that this line inspired the title of Augustine's *The City of God*. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-87/
- On dating, one Pulpit homily prefers Hezekiah's time, after Assyria's defeat, when nations brought gifts to Jerusalem. It thinks the returned exiles were too exclusive to have written something this generous. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-87.html
- The Treasury of Scripture Knowledge instead dates it to the return from exile. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rsv/psalms/87-1.html

**v. 4: Rahab, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, Cush**

*Traditional reading*
- "Rahab" is a name for Egypt (Pulpit, citing Ps 89:10 and Isa 51:9). The word literally means "pride." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-87.html
- This Rahab is spelled differently in Hebrew from Rahab of Jericho. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/87-4.htm
- A Bible Hub article suggests the name still calls to mind the Jericho Rahab's conversion. https://biblehub.com/q/Rahab_Babylon_s_role_in_Psalm_87_4.htm
- Guzik, quoting Boice: "know Me" means a saving relationship with God, not just admitting He exists. Gentiles could always be counted among God's people, as Ruth and Naaman were. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-87/
- Pulpit Commentary: the Hebrew has no word for "man." It is better read as "nation." The nations are grafted into Zion, and have a second birth there. https://biblehub.com/psalms/87-4.htm
- Matthew Henry hears God saying He will count them His people when they shall receive the gospel of Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/87-4.html
- Spurgeon: Zion's old enemies are born again and become her friends. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps087.cfm

*Where readers differ*
- **Who is "I"?** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (Presbyterian) says God speaks. Barnes thinks the "I" is the psalmist. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/87-4.htm
- **Are the nations converted, or just compared with Zion?** Clarke (Methodist) reads it as a comparison: being born in those famous places is no privilege next to being born in Jerusalem. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/87-4.html Ellicott admits that at first glance the psalm looks like praise of Jerusalem as a birthplace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/87.htm Calvin, Henry, Spurgeon and the Pulpit Commentary all read it as the nations actually being brought in. https://www.ccel.org/study/Psalm_87:1-5

**v. 5: "This one and that one were born in her"**

*Traditional reading*
- Calvin: the Egyptians and others weren't born in Zion naturally but are grafted in by adoption. Since we enter the church by a second birth, "born" is the right word. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/87-5.html
- Gill: "men of all sorts," Jews and Gentiles, in great numbers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/87-5.html
- Pulpit Commentary: verse 4 spoke of nations and verse 5 of individuals. It links "the Most High will establish her" with Matthew 16:18. https://biblehub.com/psalms/87-5.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch: the Hebrew phrase means one after another without end, a countless crowd. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/87-5.htm
- Clarke: being born in Zion is an honour, but being born from above is a far greater one. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/87-5.html
- Ellicott takes verse 5 as a contrast with verse 4: natives of Jerusalem have the prouder boast. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/87-5.htm

*Catholic and Septuagint readings*
- The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) reads "Zion, mother." Guzik notes Paul had this in mind in Galatians 4:26 ("the Jerusalem above… is the mother of us all"). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-87/
- Augustine (his Psalm 86, because the Latin numbering differs): the "man born in her" is Christ, who founded the city He would be born in, just as He created the mother He would be born of. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801087.htm
- Haydock's Catholic commentary: Zion gave birth to the Man-God. It says only the Church fulfils this prophecy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/psalms-86.html
- Calvin knew this Christ-centred reading. He notes Christian teachers had been almost unanimous in applying the words to Christ. https://www.ccel.org/study/Psalm_87:1-5

**v. 6: "The LORD will record in the register of the peoples"**

*Traditional reading*
- Pulpit Commentary: God will enrol every individual from the converted nations as a full citizen. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-87.html
- A Pulpit homily ties the full census to Christ's return. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-87.html
- Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik): God's census will include many we would have left out and leave out many we would have counted. Guzik links the register to Hebrews 12:22–23. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-87/
- Bob Utley (bible.org): the picture is the citizen lists kept by ancient Near Eastern cities. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-87
- Piper (Desiring God): the Most High builds this heavenly Zion by declaring, freely and with saving effect, "This one was born there." https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/out-of-zion-the-perfection-of-beauty-god-shines-forth

*Where readers differ*
- Barnes (Presbyterian) draws a different lesson: God will in the main take his people from among those who have been born in the church. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/87-6.html
- Matthew Henry describes two kinds of birth here: born in God's house, and born again of His Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/87-6.html

**v. 7: "All my springs of joy are in You"**

*Traditional reading*
- The verse is hard to read. The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary calls it generally acknowledged to be a very difficult one. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/87-7.html
- Pulpit Commentary: the Hebrew is literally "singers as well as dancers." It pictures the converted nations arriving in procession. It also mentions Cheyne's suggestion that the verse may be a fragment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-87.html
- Spurgeon: where the church grows through many conversions, the joy becomes exuberant. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps087.cfm

*Where readers differ: who or what is "You"?*
- **God.** Guzik, following Kidner, says the grammar allows Zion or God but prefers God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-87/ Coffman agrees. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/87-7.html
- **Zion / the church and its worship (Methodist).** Wesley reads "in thee" as Zion or the church, through which mercy and grace flow. Benson (also Methodist) says blessings come through the preached word and the ordinances. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/87-7.html
- **Fountains of salvation.** Keil and Delitzsch, following Isaiah 12:3, say the nations will say this of the city of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/87-7.html
- **Descendants (Anglican).** Ellicott reads "springs" as offspring: "All my offspring is in Thee." The boast of being born in Zion carries on to one's children. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/87-7.htm
- **Joy in God's house (Baptist).** Gill sees the church's joy over Jews and Gentiles being converted. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/87-7.html
- **Instruments or dancers?** Calvin says it hardly matters which translation you choose. The point is that God's praise will sound in Zion without end. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol10/htm/xxii.iii.htm
